{"id": "1:7/q35", "question": "How is this verse counted within al-Fātiḥa?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "1:7/q35/p1", "position": "Count the basmala and combine the closing words as one verse", "reasons": "BAGHAWI-FULL: All agree the Fatiha has seven verses, but those counting the basmala begin the final verse at ‘those You favored’; others begin it at ‘not those under wrath.’ BAGHAWI-FULL: Those counting the basmala cite its Quranic-script placement and a report from Ibn Abbas through Saʿid b. Jubayr: it is the seventh of the seven oft-repeated verses. | mentions 15:87 IBNATIYYA: Consensus counts al-Fātiḥa as seven verses, ending them respectively at العالمين, الرحيم, الدين, نستعين, المستقيم, أنعمت عليهم, and ولا الضالين; he says the weak dispute over the basmala was discussed earlier. TABRISI reporting النبي: The Prophet says God bestowed the Opening of the Book from a treasure of Paradise, including the basmala and the verse about people turning away when God alone is mentioned. | mentions 17:46 RAZI-FULL reporting أم سلمة عن النبي: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha while counting the basmala as its first verse, followed by the rest of its verses. RAZI-FULL: The seven-verse count supports al-Shafi'i's division, with the basmala as one verse and the final phrase as one; Abu Hanifa denies the basmala verse and splits that final phrase, a weak view for Razi. ABUHAYYAN: Abū Ḥayyān concludes that the sūra is seven verses by consensus apart from disregarded dissent; Meccan and Kufan counters differ over whether the basmala or صراط الذين is an āya, while ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd counts eight and Ḥusayn al-Juʿfī six. ABUHAYYAN: Reports about the sūra's letter count, supposed occasions of revelation, basmala's merit, and many titles are not necessarily causes of revelation or core tafsīr; only sound Prophetic clarification, occasions, and abrogation are indispensable to tafsīr. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting الجمهور المكيون والكوفيون: The Meccan and Kufan majority count the basmala as a verse and do not count “whom You favored” separately; other counters reverse those choices. BURHAN: Al-Shafiʿi counts the basmala and makes the rest of 1:7 one verse; Abu Hanifa omits the basmala and divides its two phrases. Both count seven verses, but al-Shafiʿi's division better preserves the endings because anʿamta ʿalayhim does not match prior endings. DURR-FULL reporting أم سلمة: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited the Fātiḥa including the basmala and called it seven verses. ITQAN reporting أبو ميسرة عمرو بن شرحبيل: A mursal report with trustworthy narrators recounts Muhammad telling Khadija he feared the voice he heard; Waraqa advised him to listen, then taught him the opening of al-Fatiha from the basmala through “those astray.” | mentions 1:1, 1:7 ITQAN reporting الإمام فخر الدين وغيره: Qur'anic verse endings fall into only two kinds, identical or near-sounding; their similarity supports counting al-Fatiha as seven verses with the basmala and treating the final phrase as one verse. IBNASHUR-FULL: The verse division differs by region: Medinans exclude the basmala and count “those You favored” as a verse; Meccans and Kufans include the basmala and combine that phrase with its verse; Hasan counts both separately."}, {"id": "1:7/q35/p2", "position": "Seven verses", "reasons": "TAB reporting أهل الإلحاد الطاعنون في القرآن: Critics ask why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses when, they argue, the meaning of its remaining verses is already contained in “Master of Judgment Day” and “You alone we worship and ask for help.” TAB-FULL: Answering why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses if two contain its meanings: earlier scriptures each included only some meanings, while the Qur'an gathers all of them for Muhammad's community and adds many more. IBNATIYYA-FULL: There is agreement that al-Fatiha has seven verses, counted as al-ʿalamin, al-Rahim, al-Din, nastaʿin, al-mustaqim, anʿamta ʿalayhim, and wa-la al-dallin; the earlier discussion noted anomalous contrary reports. RAZI-FULL: Al-Fatiha has seven verses to counter these seven vices; its opening three names answer the three basic vices, and the Qur'an and moral traits branch from these foundations. QUTB-ZILAL: Al-Fatiha is Meccan and has seven verses; Muslims recite it at least seventeen times daily, more with voluntary prayers, and may repeat it without limit."}, {"id": "1:7/q35/p3", "position": "Six verses", "reasons": "DURR reporting أبو هريرة: Abū Hurayra identifies the phrase as the sixth verse. {"id": "1:7/q37", "question": "What does the divine report say about the servant's closing request?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "1:7/q37/p1", "position": "God answers the recitation and grants the servant's closing petition", "reasons": "MUQATIL reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet related that God divided this sūra between Himself and the servant: praise is thanks, the two mercy names are praise, the King verse is glorification, and the rest belongs to the servant; seeking help is God's special acknowledgment of the servant's plea. TAB reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said God answers the worshipper's recitation: He calls al-ḥamdu praise, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm commendation, Mālik Yawm al-Dīn glorification, and the rest of the surah the servant's share. BAGHAWI reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: In a qudsi report, God divides prayer between Himself and His servant and answers each part of al-Fatiha; Baghawi grades it sahih. | mentions 1:4 RAZI-FULL reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي: In the divided-prayer report, God calls the basmala glorification, al-Hamd praise, the two mercy names extolling, the Master of Judgment entrustment, and the remaining response a sharing and a request granted. RAZI-FULL: A divine report says God remembers a servant in a gathering better than the servant's; the angels then long to visit, and the worshipper greets them on both sides. NASAFI reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي: Abu Hurayra reports God’s dialogue dividing the Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise, glorification, and exaltation belong to God; the worshipper’s request for guidance and the response to it belong to the servant, while worship and aid are shared. IBNKATHIR reporting الله تعالى: In a divine report, God divides the prayer between Himself and His servant, responds to each recited section, calls 1:5 shared between them, and grants the servant's request. BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification. BIQAI-FULL reporting أبو هريرة: In the authentic report in Muslim and the four Sunan, God says the Fatiha is divided between Himself and His servant: He answers praise, glorification and worship, and grants the servant's final requests. DURR-FULL reporting الله عز وجل: In Abū Hurayra's report, God says the prayer is divided between Him and His servant: the opening praise is His, the middle is shared, and the servant receives what he asks in the remainder. ITQAN reporting الطيبي: Al-Tibi divides the Fatiha’s religious knowledge into foundations (God and attributes, prophethood, resurrection), branches (worship), ethical perfection and seeking the path, and accounts of earlier peoples with promise and threat. | mentions 1:2, 1:4, 1:6, 1:7 QUTB-ZILAL reporting رسول الله: Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who receives what he asks. IBNASHUR-FULL reporting النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم: A hadith in both Sahihs from Abu Hurayra has God divide prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each portion of al-Fatiha and granting the servant's request. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7 TABATABAI reporting النبي: The Prophet transmits God's division of al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: each phrase receives divine acknowledgement and a tailored promise of blessing, mercy, ease of judgment, reward, help, and fulfillment of the servant's requests. ABUDAWUD reporting الله تعالى: In a hadith qudsi transmitted by Abu Hurayra, God divides al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise and glorification receive divine responses, worship is mutual, and the guidance petition belongs to the servant. MALIK reporting الله تبارك وتعالى: The qudsi report assigns the final plea for guidance to the servant and says the servant receives what he asks. MUSLIM reporting الله تعالى: When the servant asks for the guided path and names those favored rather than those under anger or astray, Allah says this request is for the servant and grants what was asked. NASAI reporting رسول الله: The same report assigns the servant’s request for the favored path, away from those under wrath and those astray, to the servant; God grants what the servant asks. TIRMIDHI reporting الله تعالى: In the divine report the Opening is divided into halves: praise belongs to God, the central pledge of worship and seeking help is shared, and its closing requests belong to the worshipper, who receives what he asks."}]}
